Main.sentence: The ___E:United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States)___ presidential library system is a nationwide network of 16 libraries administered by the Office of Presidential Libraries, which is part of the ___E:National Archives and Records Administration U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archives_and_Records_Administration)___ (NARA).

These are repositories for preserving and making available the papers, records, collections and other historical materials of ___E:every president of the United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States)___ since ___E:Herbert Hoover U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Hoover)___ , the ___E:31st president from 1929 to 1933 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Herbert_Hoover)___ .
In addition to the library services, museum exhibitions concerning the presidency are displayed.

Although recognized as having historical significance, before the mid-20th century presidential papers and effects were generally understood to be the private property of the president. ___E:Franklin D. Roosevelt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt)___ (32nd president, 1933–1945) proposed to leave his papers to the public in a building donated by him on his Hyde Park, New York, estate.
Since then, a series of laws established the public keeping of documents and the presidential library system.
These laws now seek to create a public archive library for each presidential term, with NARA taking control of the library documents immediately upon expiration of a term of office.
Additional provisions govern when the documents are made available to the public.
While not sanctioned and maintained by NARA, libraries have also been organized for several presidents who preceded Hoover and the official start of the Presidential Library Office.
The library sites are sometimes referred to as presidential centers .

Since the ___E:Barack Obama Presidential Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama_Presidential_Center)___ (44th president, ___E:2009–2017 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Barack_Obama)___ ), it operates under a new model, providing fully digitized records that are preserved, and administered by NARA with archival materials lent to the privately operated Presidential Center for display.

For every president since ___E:Herbert Hoover U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Hoover)___ , presidential libraries have been established in each president's home state in which documents, artifacts, gifts of state and museum exhibits are maintained that relate to the former president's life and career both political and professional.
Each library also provides an active series of public programs.

When a president leaves office, the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) establishes a presidential materials project to house and index the documents until they are required by law to make them available to the public, either in a library building or digitally.

The first presidential library is the ___E:Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library and Museum U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt_Presidential_Library_and_Museum)___ , dedicated on June 30, 1941. The ___E:George W. Bush Presidential Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush_Presidential_Center)___ became the thirteenth on May 1, 2013.
The ___E:National Archives and Records Administration U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archives_and_Records_Administration)___ uses a passport to promote visiting the Presidential libraries.
When a person visits every library, NARA awards them a crystal paperweight.

The presidential library system is made up of thirteen presidential libraries operated fully, or partially, by NARA. [n 1]  Libraries and museums have been established for earlier presidents, but they are not part of the NARA presidential library system, and are operated by private foundations, historical societies, or state governments, including the ___E:James K. Polk U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_K._Polk)___ , ___E:William McKinley U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_McKinley)___ , ___E:Rutherford B. Hayes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rutherford_B._Hayes)___ , ___E:Calvin Coolidge U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvin_Coolidge)___ , ___E:Abraham Lincoln U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln)___ and ___E:Woodrow Wilson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodrow_Wilson)___ libraries.

For example, the ___E:Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln_Presidential_Library_and_Museum)___ is owned and operated by the state of ___E:Illinois U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois)___ .
The ___E:Richard Nixon Library and Birthplace U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Nixon_Presidential_Library_and_Museum)___ was not originally part of the presidential library system.

While the Nixon Presidential Materials Staff, which administers the Nixon presidential materials under the terms of the ___E:Presidential Recordings and Materials Preservation Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Recordings_and_Materials_Preservation_Act)___ , is part of NARA, the private nonprofit ___E:Richard Nixon Foundation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Nixon_Foundation)___ owned and operated the Richard Nixon Library & Birthplace.

In January 2004, Congress passed legislation that provided for the establishment of a federally operated Richard Nixon Presidential Library in ___E:Yorba Linda, California U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorba_Linda,_California)___ .

In March 2005, the ___E:Archivist of the United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archivist_of_the_United_States)___ and John Taylor, the director of the Richard Nixon Library & Birthplace Foundation, exchanged letters on the requirements to allow the Nixon Library to become the twelfth federally funded presidential library operated by NARA by 2007, while the Nixon Foundation would continue to own the campus and operate the Nixon Library complex with NARA.  On October 16, 2006, Dr. ___E:Timothy Naftali U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_Naftali)___ began his tenure as the first federal director of the Richard Nixon Library and Birthplace, and in the winter of 2006 NARA began to transfer the 30,000 presidential gifts from the Nixon Presidential Materials Staff in College Park, Maryland, to the Yorba Linda facility.
On July 11, 2007, NARA began its operations at the Nixon Library site and the facility's name was changed to Richard Nixon Presidential Library and Museum.

In May 2012, on the fiftieth anniversary of the founding of the ___E:Ulysses S. Grant U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant)___ Foundation, it selected ___E:Mississippi State University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_State_University#Mitchell_Memorial_Library)___ as the permanent location for Ulysses S. Grant's presidential library.
Historian John Simon edited Grant's letters into a 32-volume scholarly edition published by Southern Illinois University Press.

On April 30, 2013, both chambers of the ___E:North Dakota Legislative Assembly U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Dakota_Legislative_Assembly)___ passed a bill appropriating $12 million to ___E:Dickinson State University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dickinson_State_University)___ to award a grant to the Theodore Roosevelt Center for construction of a building to be named the ___E:Theodore Roosevelt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt)___ Presidential Library.
To access these funds, the Theodore Roosevelt Center must first raise $3 million from non-state sources.

Dickinson State University is also home to the ___E:Theodore Roosevelt Digital Library U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt_Digital_Library)___ which has formed partnerships with the Library of Congress and Harvard University, among other institutions.
They currently have over 25,000 items online.

On April 12, 2016, Harding 2020, a collaboration between the ___E:Harding Home U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harding_Home)___ , ___E:Ohio History Connection U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_History_Connection)___ , and ___E:Marion Technical College U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marion_Technical_College)___ , detailed plans to spend $7.3 million to establish the ___E:Warren G. Harding Presidential Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_G._Harding_Presidential_Center)___ .

Plans include restoring the Harding Home, ___E:Warren G. Harding U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_G._Harding)___ 's historic home in ___E:Marion, Ohio U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marion,_Ohio)___ , and its grounds to its 1920 appearance.
A 15,000-square-foot presidential center and museum was built adjacent to the house.

Harding's presidential papers were moved from its previous location at the Ohio History Connection's headquarters in ___E:Columbus, Ohio U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus,_Ohio)___ , to the new center.
The culmination of the work, was scheduled to be completed by the spring of 2020, to coincide with the 100th anniversary of Harding's election to the presidency.

The library was scheduled to open initially on May 23, 2020, with a formal dedication ceremony on Friday, July 17, 2020. This was then delayed until September due largely to back orders on construction materials and other issues.
Then, the ___E:COVID-19 pandemic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic)___ delayed the opening of the museum until May 12, 2021

In May 2017, it was announced that the ___E:Barack Obama Presidential Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama_Presidential_Center)___ , the planned location of the presidential library of ___E:Barack Obama U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama)___ , would not be part of the NARA system, making Obama the first president since Calvin Coolidge not to have a federally owned facility.
Instead, in a "new model" the nonprofit ___E:Obama Foundation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obama_Foundation)___ will partner with the NARA on digitization and making documents available.
It was announced that the City of Chicago would own the center.
Historically, all presidential papers were considered the personal property of the president.
Some took them at the end of their terms, others destroyed them, and many papers were scattered.

Though many pre-Hoover collections now reside in the Manuscript Division of the ___E:Library of Congress U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress)___ ,  others are split among other libraries, historical societies, and private collections.
However, many materials have been lost or (accidentally or deliberately) destroyed.

___E:Lucretia Rudolph Garfield U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucretia_Rudolph_Garfield)___ , the wife of ___E:James A. Garfield U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_A._Garfield)___ (president from March 4, 1881, until his death on September 19, 1881) added a Memorial Library wing to their family home in ___E:Mentor, Ohio U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mentor,_Ohio)___ , four years after his assassination.

The ___E:James A. Garfield National Historic Site U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_A._Garfield_National_Historic_Site)___ was operated by the ___E:National Park Service U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Park_Service)___ and the ___E:Western Reserve Historical Society U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Reserve_Historical_Society)___ until 2008 when the historical society gave over full control to the National Parks.
In 1939, President ___E:Franklin Delano Roosevelt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_Delano_Roosevelt)___ donated his personal and presidential papers to the federal government.

At the same time, Roosevelt pledged part of his estate at ___E:Hyde Park, New York U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyde_Park,_New_York)___ , to the United States, and friends of the president formed a non-profit corporation to raise funds for the construction of the library and museum building.
Roosevelt's decision stemmed from his belief that presidential papers were an important part of the national heritage and should be accessible to the public.
He asked the National Archives to take custody of his papers and other historical materials and to administer his library.

On June 30, 2013, new interactive and multimedia exhibits developed by the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) opened to the public as part of the first renovation of this library since its opening.

In 1950, ___E:Harry S. Truman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman)___ decided that he, too, would build a library to house his presidential papers and helped to galvanize congressional action.
In 1955, Congress passed the Presidential Libraries Act of 1955,  establishing a system of privately erected and federally maintained libraries.

The Act encouraged other presidents to donate their historical materials to the government and ensured the preservation of presidential papers and their availability to the people of the United States.
Under this and subsequent acts, nine more libraries have been established.
In each case, private and non-federal public sources provided the funds to build the library.
Generally, once completed the private organization turned over the libraries to the National Archives and Records Administration to operate and maintain.

The ___E:library and museum U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Nixon_Presidential_Library_and_Museum)___ founded for ___E:Richard Nixon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Nixon)___ remained privately owned and managed for many years, but his heirs ultimately reached an agreement for it to become a NARA facility.

Until 1978, presidents, scholars, and legal professionals held the view dating back to ___E:George Washington U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington)___ that the records created by the president or his staff while in office remained the personal property of the president and were his to take with him when he left office.
The first presidential libraries were built on this concept.
NARA successfully persuaded presidents to donate their historical materials to the federal government for housing in a presidential library managed by NARA.

Apart from the presidency of Richard Nixon, the handling of presidential records by NARA for the presidencies of Hoover through Carter (1929–1969, and 1973–1980) are governed by their ___E:deeds of gift U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deed_of_gift)___ , whereby the public took ownership of the records of each president.

In the wake of the ___E:Watergate scandal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watergate_scandal)___ , Congress asserted public ownership and control of materials from the Nixon White House (1969–1973), under the ___E:Presidential Recordings and Materials Preservation Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Recordings_and_Materials_Preservation_Act)___ of 1974.

The ___E:Presidential Records Act of 1978 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Records_Act_of_1978)___ established that the presidential records that document the constitutional, statutory, and ceremonial duties of the president are the property of the United States Government.
When the president leaves office, the ___E:Archivist of the United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archivist_of_the_United_States)___ assumes custody of the records.
The Act allowed for the continuation of presidential libraries as the repository for presidential records.

The ___E:Presidential Libraries Act of 1986 U:(https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/en:Presidential_Libraries_Act_of_1986)___  made additional changes to presidential libraries, requiring private endowments linked to the size of the facility.
NARA uses these endowments to offset a portion of the maintenance costs for the library.

The ___E:Presidential Historical Records Preservation Act of 2008 U:(https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/en:Presidential_Historical_Records_Preservation_Act_of_2008)___ amended ___E:44 U.S.C. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Title_44_of_the_United_States_Code)___ ___E:§ 2504 U:(https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/44/2504)___ to authorize grants for Presidential Centers of Historical Excellence.

While the libraries for presidents Hoover to George W. Bush eventually conformed to a model whereby the former president funded or fundraised and built a facility for NARA to house the library, presidents are not required to do so under the law (Nixon's was not under NARA for many years).

Nonetheless, according to NARA as of 2023, recent changes in these laws have increased significantly the amount of endowment the former president must raise, if they do decide to build a NARA owned facility.

According to NARA, not only are the digital nature of modern records changing the needs, plans, and lessening space requirements of physical storage, but the significantly increased endowment requirement may lessen the likelihood that present and future presidents will continue to build NARA facilities.

The thirteen presidential libraries maintain over 400 million pages of textual materials; nearly ten million photographs; over 15 million feet (5,000 km) of motion picture film; nearly 100,000 hours of disc, audiotape, and videotape recordings; and approximately half a million museum objects.
These varied holdings make each library a valuable source of information and a center for research on the Presidency.
The most important textual materials in each library are those created by the president and his staff in the course of performing the official duties.

Libraries also house numerous objects including family heirlooms, items collected by the president and his family, campaign memorabilia, awards, and the many gifts given to the president by American citizens and foreign dignitaries.

These gifts range in type from homemade items to valuable works of art. Curators in presidential libraries and in other museums throughout the country draw upon these collections for historical exhibits.
Other significant holdings include the personal papers and historical materials donated by individuals associated with the president.

These individuals may include ___E:Cabinet officials U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Cabinet)___ , envoys to foreign governments, political party associates, and the president's family and personal friends.
Several libraries have undertaken oral history programs that have produced tape-recorded memoirs.
A third body of materials comprises the papers accumulated by the president prior to, and following, his presidency.

Such collections include documents relating to Theodore Roosevelt's tenure as ___E:Governor of New York U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_New_York)___ and ___E:Dwight D. Eisenhower U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dwight_D._Eisenhower)___ 's long military career.

With the exception of ___E:John F. Kennedy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy)___ , ___E:Lyndon B. Johnson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyndon_B._Johnson)___ , and ___E:Jimmy Carter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter)___ , every American president since Hoover is or has chosen to be buried at his presidential library.

Kennedy is buried at ___E:Arlington National Cemetery U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington_National_Cemetery)___ ; Johnson is buried at ___E:his ranch U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyndon_B._Johnson_National_Historical_Park)___ in the hill country of Texas, west of Austin; Carter is buried near ___E:his home U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter_National_Historic_Site)___ in ___E:Plains, Georgia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plains,_Georgia)___ .

Bill Clinton will be buried at the ___E:William Jefferson Clinton Presidential Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Jefferson_Clinton_Presidential_Center)___ in Little Rock. ___E:George W. Bush U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush)___ will be buried at the ___E:George W. Bush Presidential Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush_Presidential_Center)___ in Dallas.

The future burial sites of 44th president ___E:Barack Obama U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama)___ , 45th and 47th president ___E:Donald Trump U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump)___ , and 46th president ___E:Joe Biden U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden)___ are still unknown.

Unlike all other presidents whose libraries are part of the NARA system, Ford's ___E:library U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_R._Ford_Presidential_Library)___ and ___E:museum U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_R._Ford_Presidential_Museum)___ are geographically separate buildings, located in different parts of ___E:Michigan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan)___ ; Ford is buried at his museum in ___E:Grand Rapids U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Rapids,_Michigan)___ , while the library is in ___E:Ann Arbor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ann_Arbor,_Michigan)___ .

___E:Grover Cleveland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland)___ and ___E:Woodrow Wilson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodrow_Wilson)___ left their papers to Princeton University where they may be found at the ___E:Seeley G. Mudd Manuscript Library U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seeley_G._Mudd_Manuscript_Library)___ .

The ___E:Theodore Roosevelt Association U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt_Association)___ collected ___E:Theodore Roosevelt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt)___ 's papers and donated them to ___E:Harvard University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University)___ in 1943, where they reside at its Widener and Houghton libraries.

___E:James Buchanan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Buchanan)___ left his papers to the ___E:Historical Society of Pennsylvania U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_Society_of_Pennsylvania)___ in Philadelphia, where they may still be found.

The Papers of Andrew Jackson is a project sponsored by the ___E:University of Tennessee at Knoxville U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Tennessee_at_Knoxville)___ to collect ___E:Andrew Jackson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Jackson)___ 's papers on microfilm.

A microfilm edition of ___E:Martin Van Buren U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren)___ 's papers was produced at ___E:Pennsylvania State University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_State_University)___ in 1987; a digital edition of the ___E:Papers of Martin Van Buren U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papers_of_Martin_Van_Buren)___ is being produced at ___E:Cumberland University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumberland_University)___ .
A similar project is underway on behalf of ___E:James Madison U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Papers_of_James_Madison)___ by the Universities of Virginia and Chicago.
For many presidents, especially before the development of the NARA system, substantial collections may be found in multiple private and public collections.

Until the Obama Administration's library is ready for service, its papers are being held in a facility in ___E:Hoffman Estates, Illinois U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoffman_Estates,_Illinois)___ , and except for classified materials are available through ___E:FOIA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_Information_Act_(United_States))___ since 2023.
